lesson.title: Wi-Fi Channels: Slicing Up Limited Airwaves
lesson.summary: A Wi-Fi channel is a specific slice of radio frequency spectrum that an access point transmits on, and because nearby channels overlap and interfere, choosing channels wisely is essential to making multiple networks coexist.
lesson.body:
Radio spectrum is a genuinely limited, shared physical resource, unlike, say, the number of Ethernet cables a building can run. Regulators worldwide set aside specific frequency bands for unlicensed use, primarily 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, and more recently 6 GHz for Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 devices, and within each band the spectrum is divided into individual channels so that multiple access points nearby can each pick a channel and, ideally, avoid stepping on each other's transmissions.

The 2.4 GHz band, used since the earliest 802.11b and 802.11g days, spans roughly 2.400 to 2.4835 GHz and is divided into channels numbered 1 through 11 in the United States, up to 13 in much of the rest of the world. Each individual channel occupies about 22 MHz of spectrum, but adjacent channel numbers are spaced only 5 MHz apart, so neighboring channels overlap substantially and interfere with each other. Only channels 1, 6, and 11 are spaced far enough apart to be fully non-overlapping in the standard 2.4 GHz layout, which is why administrators are almost always told to stick to 1, 6, or 11 rather than picking channels in between.

The 5 GHz band offers far more usable spectrum and many more non-overlapping 20 MHz channels, and it also supports channel bonding, combining adjacent channels into wider 40, 80, or even 160 MHz channels to push more data through at once at the cost of using more spectrum per access point. Higher frequency signals like 5 GHz and 6 GHz also attenuate faster through walls and travel shorter distances than 2.4 GHz, a real physical tradeoff: 2.4 GHz covers more area but with less capacity and more interference from other devices like microwave ovens and Bluetooth accessories, while 5 and 6 GHz offer far more capacity but weaker range.

Consider an apartment building where every unit's router defaults to 2.4 GHz channel 6 out of the box. In a building with twenty apartments all inheriting that same default, every resident's access point transmits on the identical, or a heavily overlapping, slice of spectrum, and everyone's throughput suffers from constant contention and interference, even though each individual network technically works fine in isolation. A network administrator resolving this would manually spread nearby access points across channels 1, 6, and 11, physically separated where possible, exactly the kind of channel planning that determines how clean the roaming handoffs described in the ESS concept actually feel in practice.

Even with the best channel planning, every device sharing a channel is still contending for the same limited airtime, using the collision avoidance approach from the wireless LAN concept, and one particular problem with that contention, devices that cannot hear each other but both interfere at a common access point, motivates the RTS/CTS mechanism covered next.
